$comment: WHAT EVERY PUBLISHED ASSET MUST CONTAIN — the list, in one place, read by two readers.
Written 2026-09-22, after v2.12.0 shipped with two of its headline claims untrue of the
zips people downloaded. That release was the one that found four runtime payloads staged
into $(OutDir) and never into the publish, and it fixed the MSBuild correctly. But two of
the four are third-party binaries that are not in the repository, every item is Exists()-
guarded so a build without them succeeds in silence, and the release is built by GitHub
Actions, which did not have them. The fix landed on one machine and not on the artifact.
PublishStagingParityTests cannot catch that and is not at fault: parsing the csproj as XML
verifies the RULES, and whether the file exists on the release runner is a different
question that no test reading this repository can answer. The check has to be on the
artifact. scripts/verify_release_payloads.py applies this file to the built zips inside the
release job, before anything is published.
The same file is read by ReleasePayloadManifestTests, which asserts that everything named
here is also staged by the csproj that owns it — so the two halves cannot drift: a payload
added to the build without being added to the artifact check, or vice versa, is a test
failure rather than a discovery made by reading a published zip six months later.

required.why: without it PluginTrustPolicy.RequireTrusted enforces an empty allow-list and refuses all 33 plugin DLLs — the market dropdown offers only the built-in providers, with nothing saying why
the provider and analytics plugins the manifest above vouches for

required.why: NVDA-direct speech. The chart is a native SkiaSharp canvas over the BlazorWebView, so a reader focused on the chart is not reading the DOM and the ARIA live-region fallback cannot reach it. NO DLL MEANS THE CHART IS SILENT — which is the whole application. NV Access renamed the file, so either spelling counts.

the tactile SDK entry point WindowsDotPadNative binds its exports on; absent, the driver logs 'NativeLibrary.TryLoad failed ... Tactile DISABLED' and falls back to NullDotPadNative while the Braille tab keeps rendering, which is the worst of the two
the braille translator behind DOT_PAD_BRAILLE_DISPLAY. The SDK LoadLibrary's it by name and reports DOT_ERROR_LIBLOUIS_DLL_COULD_NOT_LOAD when it is missing.

the LibLouis translation tables. The SDK calls lou_setDataPath at a \tables directory beside itself and names 35 specific .ctb/.utb files; without them there is no text-to-braille. 419 files at 3.0.0.
the SDK's text-to-braille engine, LoadLibrary'd by DotPadSDK at runtime
a STATIC import of TTBEngine.dll — read out of its PE import table, so TTBEngine cannot load without it beside it
a Dot Pad SDK module its siblings expect beside them
the MeCab config the SDK reads at init

DotPadSDK-3.0.0.dll STATICALLY imports MSVCP140/VCRUNTIME140/VCRUNTIME140_1 — read out of its PE import table. A .NET publish carries none of them, so on a machine without the VC++ 2015-2022 redistributable NativeLibrary.TryLoad fails and tactile is silently disabled: the exact symptom shipping the SDK is meant to end.
see msvcp140.dll

why: v2.11.0's Windows app was precompiled and v2.12.0's was not, with nothing in the repo
setting PublishReadyToRun either way — an implicit default moved under us, and the only
trace was the zip falling 148.4 -> 130.8 MB while gaining seven files. It costs startup
and first-use JIT on the head with the slowest start already. The property is now set
explicitly in the csproj; this asserts the bytes rather than the intent, by reading each
PE's CLI header for a non-empty ManagedNativeHeader.
